title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Maya Chen
body:
Purpose
This page defines Redwood Inference’s SRE standards for SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, recommended operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended for on-call SREs, service owners, and engineering managers responsible for production reliability.

Scope
Applies to all customer-facing inference services and their control-plane components (request router, model-serving clusters, KV cache, metrics pipeline). Internal-only tools (dev sandboxes) should align where practical but may use relaxed SLOs.

Document structure
- SLO definitions and tiering
- Error budget policy and burn actions
- Capacity planning and forecasting
- Incident classification and review process
- Operational tooling and dashboards
- Canonical runbooks (examples)
- Governance, cadence and owners

1) SLO definitions and tiering
Overview
We operate a tiered SLO model mapped to customer plans and internal components. Each service must publish SLOs and a measurement query in Prometheus/Grafana or datadog. SRE owns platform SLOs; product owners own feature-level SLOs.

Service tiers (examples)
- Critical: Redwood API control plane (request routing, auth), Dedicated entry / model fallback path. Target availability: 99.95% monthly.
- Standard: Model inference endpoints for hosted API. Target availability: 99.9% monthly; P99 generation latency ≤ 500 ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens) for the first 95% of requests.
- Development / Non-production: lower SLOs (99% / best-effort) and annotated as non-customer impacting.

Metrics (primary SLOs to publish)
- Availability / Success rate: HTTP 2xx or domain-specific success code. Query example text: "ratio(requests{status=~\"2..\"} / requests_total) over a 30d window".
- Latency: P50/P95/P99 measured at the request boundary (router->response). Record both "time-to-first-token" and "full-response-time".
- Correctness: Model-level checks (synthetic prompt tests) measured via evaluation harness; threshold defined per model onboarding doc.

Required SLO metadata per service (must be published as a confluence service page)
- SLO name (availability / latency / correctness)
- SLO target and measurement window (e.g., 99.9% monthly)
- Measurement query or source (Prometheus query or Datadog monitor id)
- Error budget (allowed failures in window, in minutes/percent)
- Owner, primary on-call, and escalation contact

2) Error budget policy and burn actions
Definitions
- Error budget: allowed amount of objective violations (1 - SLO) over the rolling window. We compute both absolute and burn rate.
- Burn rate: the rate at which a service is consuming its error budget relative to elapsed time in the window. A burn rate of 2 means twice the expected consumption.

Thresholds and automated actions (standard)
- Normal (burn rate < 1): normal operations.
- Elevated (burn rate >= 1 for 1 hour): PagerDuty notification to service owner; require on-call to acknowledge within 30 min.
- High (burn rate >= 3 sustained for 15 minutes): Launch incident process (see incident playbook). Notify product manager and infra lead.
- Critical (error budget exhausted or burn rate >= 6 for 5 minutes): Immediate rollback/fallback to safe model variant or capacity increase; block planned feature rollouts until budget is recovered.

Operational controls tied to error budget
- Canary and feature rollout freezes: If error budget < 30% remaining, freeze all canaries and A/B rollouts for the affected service until budget recovered.
- Cost vs reliability trade decisions: Product managers and SREs must approve any quantization/optimization that has a >0.5% expected SLO impact while error budget < 50%.

3) Capacity planning and forecasting
Goals
Ensure sufficient headroom to meet SLOs under normal and expected peak usage while minimizing waste and respecting cost targets.

Inputs
- QPS and token throughput (historical 90/95/99 percentiles by hour).
- Model sequence length distribution (tokens per request) by workload.
- Tail latency contribution from KV cache misses, hot-model effects, and cold-starts.
- Scheduled events: releases, marketing spikes, partner integrations.

Capacity model (summary)
- Convert forecasted token QPS into GPU-second demand using measured tokens/sec per GPU for each model variant (lookup in quantization-profiles).
- Add SLO buffer: target 20% baseline headroom for hosted API; 30% for Dedicated when SLA requires >99.95%.
- Add emergency buffer (burst) config: autoscale policies + reserved warm workers to handle sudden 2x traffic spikes for up to 10 mins.

Capacity runbook steps (quarterly and weekly)
- Weekly: run 7-day headroom report (owner: capacity on-call) showing utilization, predicted risk windows, and recommended policy changes.
- Quarterly: full capacity forecast for next quarter including model onboarding plans, retirement of legacy models, and hardware / region expansion asks. Submit to infra planning and finance.

Autoscaling guardrails
- Prefer horizontal scaling with graceful shedding over aggressive vertical provisioning.
- Apply rate limits and priority queuing by customer tier.
- Ensure autoscaling cooldowns are tuned to avoid oscillation (recommend 2-5 minute cooldown for instance counts).

4) Incident classification and review process
Incident priorities
- Sev1 (SEV1): Customer-facing outage with widespread impact (affects >5% of traffic or critical control plane failure). Time to acknowledge: 5 minutes. Postmortem required within 72 hours.
- Sev2 (SEV2): Degraded service affecting fewer customers or increased latency beyond P95 targets. Acknowledge within 30 minutes. Post-incident review within 7 days.
- Sev3 (SEV3): Minor issue or single-customer impact with workaround. Documented in runbook; triage during normal cadence.

Run of incident review (postmortem)
- Owner: incident commander (IC) writes the postmortem and assigns reviewers.
- Template: summary, timeline, impact (quantified against SLOs), root cause, contributing factors, immediate remediation, long-term actions, owner and ETA.
- Classification: actionable | learning-only. Actionable items must be tracked in JIRA with owners and due dates; SRE lead reviews overdue items weekly.
- Blamelessness: focus on systems and processes; avoid naming individuals as root cause.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards
Canonical tools (current stack)
- Metrics + alerting: Prometheus + Thanos for long-term metrics, Grafana for dashboards, Alertmanager for routing.
- Tracing: Tempo / Jaeger for distributed traces.
- Logs: Loki for service logs; Sumo/Datadog retained for long-tail analysis where required by contracts.
- Error/exception tracking: Sentry for control-plane services.
- Oncall and escalation: PagerDuty and Slack for comms (oncall channel naming convention: #ops-<service>-oncall).
- Incident coordination: runbooks in Confluence, status updates via Statuspage for customers.

Recommended dashboards and alerts
- SLO dashboard per service (availability, latency percentiles, error budget remaining) with 30d window.
- Capacity dashboard (GPU utilization, queue lengths, batch sizes).
- Synthetic checks: global and regional canaries that exercise model inference with a set of canonical prompts every 1-5 minutes.
- Alert thresholds: availability drop >0.5% in 5m, p99 latency spike >2x baseline sustained for 3m, error budget burn rate >3.

6) Canonical runbooks (examples)
Runbook: High latency on model inference (p99 > target)
- Step 0: Acknowledge pager and update Slack channel.
- Step 1: Check SLO dashboard and recent deploys (time filter +/- 15m). Owner: oncall.
- Step 2: Check GPU utilization and queue length in capacity dashboard. If GPUs at 95%+: consider scaling up pool or enabling burst workers.
- Step 3: Look for recent model rollouts or quantization changes; if present, revert to previous model variant and monitor error budget.
- Step 4: If root cause is cache misses, flush or warm KV cache for affected prefixes and validate synthetic checks.
- Step 5: If traffic surge from a single customer, apply rate limit or priority queueing to tail traffic.
- Step 6: If cause unknown after 20 minutes, escalate to runtime team and open a debug session (link to ephemeral Jupyter or debug playground).
- Recovery: Confirm p99 < target for 30 minutes before declaring recovered.

Runbook: Model GPU OOM / OOM kills
- Step 0: Pause incoming traffic to affected worker group via router fallback rule.
- Step 1: Inspect pod/container OOM logs and dmesg for out-of-memory events.
- Step 2: Check model batch sizes and token length distribution causing peak memory. Temporarily reduce max batch size and enable per-request truncation for long sequences.
- Step 3: Roll back recent model config changes or quantization that increased memory usage.
- Step 4: For persistent OOM, scale up instance type (larger GPU) or switch to model variant with lower memory footprint and note cost impact.

Runbook: Control-plane auth failures impacting routing
- Step 0: Acknowledge and find IC.
- Step 1: Fallback to cached tokens/leases or secondary auth provider if configured.
- Step 2: Roll keys / refresh tokens following security playbook if root cause is credential expiration.
- Step 3: Notify security and compliance for any credentials compromise.

7) Reliability initiatives and governance
Quarterly reliability initiatives
- Each quarter, SRE and product identify 3 reliability initiatives (owner + success metrics). Examples: improve p99 latency for short prompts by 20%, reduce cold-start rate by 50%, or reduce error budget burn by platform re-architecture.
- Initiative tracking: tracked in roadmap and reviewed in SRE weekly sync.

Monthly governance and cadence
- Weekly SRE sync: status of active incidents, error budget heatmap, and capacity risks.
- Monthly SLO review: owners present SLO status and any proposed SLO changes to SRE leadership.
- Quarterly reliability review: cross-team meeting with product, infra, and growth to review initiative outcomes.

Ownership and contacts
- SRE lead: Ravi Kumar (primary contact for governance).
- Oncall rotation: documented in PagerDuty and team calendar; every service must list primary and secondary on the Confluence service page.

Appendices
- Appendix A: Example Prometheus queries (listed on the service page).
- Appendix B: Incident postmortem template (link).
- Appendix C: Capacity forecasting spreadsheet template (link).

Change history
- 2024-08-15: initial baseline published.
- 2025-06-10: added error budget burn thresholds and canary freeze policy.
- 2026-02-28: updated capacity headroom recommendations and runbook steps for GPU OOMs.

If you are a service owner without a published SLO page, create one following the SRE SLO template and schedule a review with SRE within two weeks. For questions or exceptions, contact the SRE lead or open a ticket in the SRE backlog.
